html:
The First Council of Nicaea was a meeting of Christian bishops called by the Roman emperor Constantine the Great in 325 at Nicaea, today's Iznik in Turkey. It was the first council of the whole Church, and it agreed the first version of the Nicene Creed, the definition of mainstream Christian belief.

Constantine had recently made Christianity legal and favoured it. He wanted a united Church, but Christians were split by an argument about who Jesus was. Arius, a priest in Alexandria, taught that the Son was created by God the Father and so was not fully equal to him. His bishop, and the young deacon Athanasius, said the Son was fully God, as eternal as the Father.

At least two hundred bishops came, almost all from the eastern half of the empire. The council ruled against Arius:

  • It declared the Son "of one substance" with the Father, a key phrase of the Nicene Creed.
  • Arius and the bishops who refused to sign were exiled.
  • It set a common way to fix the date of Easter and made rules for how the Church was run.

The argument did not end there. Later emperors sometimes favoured Arius's side, and the Goths who converted in this period took Arian Christianity with them into western Europe. The First Council of Constantinople in 381 confirmed and expanded the creed, and that version is still said in churches today. Nicaea set the pattern of emperors and bishops settling belief together for the Roman Empire.
